Definition: Whether individuals can view their data held in the ID database and see how it has been accessed
Comments: The Data Protection Act 2023 grants data subjects the right to access, request correction or deletion of their data, block access, and oppose usage for specific purposes (Section 19). The SeyID platform allows users to view their own NIN, date of birth, and ID details in the virtual card. The DPA also grants rights to data portability and rectification. Citizens can request copies of their civil registration records through CertExpress.
revision_notes: Sources fetched and confirmed: Data Protection Act 2023 (Section 19, Part V) grants data subjects rights of access, rectification and deletion; SeyID Terms of Use (Section 6, 'SeyID Profile Data Usage') confirm all registered users can view their personal data profile, including NIN, name, date of birth and photo sourced from the National Population Database. Score of 2 (Yes) is well supported. Confirmed, no change.
revised_comments: Individuals can view the personal data held about them through the SeyID platform, whose Terms of Use grant all registered users access to their profile data, including NIN, name, date of birth and photograph, sourced from the National Population Database. The Data Protection Act 2023 additionally provides a statutory right to access, request correction of, and delete personal data, alongside portability and rectification rights, and citizens may obtain copies of civil registration records through the CertExpress portal.

Definition: Whether the ID authority and system are subject to general oversight of the courts and judicial review
Value Name: Yes, but not specific to ID
Comments: Seychelles has general judicial oversight through its courts, and the Data Protection Act 2023 provides rights of appeal against enforcement notices to the Commission (Section 13). The Constitution (Article 20) recognises the right to privacy. However, no ID-specific judicial oversight mechanisms (such as dedicated ID ombudsman, ID appeals tribunal, or constitutional court review of ID-specific issues) have been identified in available sources.
revision_notes: Sources fetched and confirmed: the Data Protection Act 2023 provides a general right of appeal to the courts against Commission enforcement notices (Section 13), and Article 20 of the Constitution recognises the right to privacy. A further search of Information Commission publications (Annual Report 2025, Strategic Plan 2026-2028) found no ID-specific judicial mechanism such as a dedicated ID tribunal or ombudsman. Score of 2 (general oversight, not ID-specific) confirmed, no change.
revised_comments: Seychelles' digital identity system is subject to general judicial oversight rather than an ID-specific mechanism. The Constitution (Article 20) recognises the right to privacy, and the Data Protection Act 2023 provides a statutory right of appeal to the courts against enforcement notices issued by the Information Commission. No dedicated ID appeals tribunal or ID-specific judicial review mechanism has been established.

Definition: Whether procedural rules for collection, storage, and sharing of ID-related personal data are publicly available and established
Comments: The Data Protection Act 2023 establishes partial data sharing rules: it sets consent requirements, data minimisation principles, purpose limitation, and cross-border transfer safeguards (Seychelles is the first African country to recognise the CBPR mechanism). The SeyID eKYC explicitly requires customer approval before sending identity data to service providers. However, a comprehensive published data-sharing framework specifically for the identity system has not been identified; the DPA's 18-month transition period runs until mid-2025.
revision_notes: Original sources verified as valid and read. A further search found the SeyID Privacy Policy and Terms of Use (Section 6, 'SeyID Profile Data Usage'), both fetched and read, which publish a detailed, ID-system-specific data governance framework: an explicit table of data fields collected and their source (National Population Database versus user-provided), consent-gated sharing with integrated third-party service providers, and storage/retention terms. Combined with the Data Protection Act 2023's general consent, minimisation, purpose-limitation and cross-border transfer rules (Sections 15-47), this constitutes a fully published, ID-specific data-sharing framework rather than only a partial one. Score revised upward from 2 (Partially available) to 3 (Fully available).
revised_comments: Procedural rules for the collection, storage and sharing of digital ID-related personal data are fully publicly available. The SeyID platform publishes a Privacy Policy and Terms of Use that set out exactly which data fields are collected, their source (the National Population Database or user input), the consent-based mechanism for sharing data with integrated third-party service providers, and storage arrangements. This ID-specific documentation sits alongside the Data Protection Act 2023, which establishes general consent, data-minimisation, purpose-limitation and cross-border transfer safeguards enforced by the Information Commission.

Definition: Whether national data protection legislation exists and covers personal data linked to the ID system
Comments: Seychelles enacted the Data Protection Act 2023 (Act 24 of 2023), signed by President Ramkalawan on 19 December 2023 and published on 22 December 2023. It replaces the Data Protection Act 2003 which was never implemented in practice. The 2023 Act aligns with GDPR principles, covers rights of data subjects, creates enforcement mechanisms including fines, mandates data protection impact assessments for high-risk activities, and provides for cross-border data transfer safeguards.
revision_notes: Sources fetched and confirmed: Data Protection Act 2023 (Act 24 of 2023), assented 19 December 2023, gazetted 22 December 2023, confirmed in force by Appleby (25 March 2024) and the Information Commission website. Repeals the unimplemented 2003 Act. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed, no change.
revised_comments: Seychelles has enacted comprehensive national data protection legislation, the Data Protection Act 2023 (Act 24 of 2023), assented to by President Ramkalawan on 19 December 2023 and gazetted on 22 December 2023. It repeals the earlier 2003 Act, which was never implemented, and covers personal data collected and processed by the digital ID system, including biometric and identity data held under SeyID.

Definition: Whether a Data Protection Authority or similar body regulates ID data collection and sharing by the ID system
Comments: The Data Protection Act 2023 designates the Information Commission (established under the Access to Information Act) as the competent authority to enforce data protection law. The Commission has powers to conduct investigations, audits, issue enforcement notices, impose fines up to SCR 200,000, and order suspension of data flows. This constitutes an operational data protection authority with oversight of digital identity data.
revision_notes: Sources fetched and confirmed: DPA 2023 Section 5 designates the Information Commission as the enforcing authority, with powers under Sections 6-8 to investigate, audit, issue enforcement notices and impose fines. Fresh evidence from the Information Commission's Strategic Plan 2026-2028 confirms the Commission is operationally active under its DPA mandate, having established data protection procedures and conducted compliance work since 2023, with compliance checks and investigations planned through 2028. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed, no change.
revised_comments: Data collection and sharing by Seychelles' digital ID system is regulated by the Information Commission, designated under the Data Protection Act 2023 as the country's data protection authority. The Commission has powers to conduct investigations and compliance audits, issue enforcement notices, and impose administrative fines, and its 2026-2028 Strategic Plan confirms it is actively enforcing the Act, including through compliance checks and investigations, alongside its pre-existing access-to-information mandate.

Definition: Whether formal legislation (act, law, regulation) governs digital identity including identification acts, digital ID laws, or equivalent legislation
Comments: Seychelles has a well-established legal framework for identity. The Civil Status Act governs civil registration and identity management (originally 1893, updated to 2022). The National Identity Number system has been compulsory by law since 1995. The Data Protection Act 2023 (Act 24 of 2023) enacted December 2023 provides a comprehensive legal framework covering digital data processing, privacy rights, and oversight. The Minister for Finance announced in November 2022 budget that the digital ID system is legally operational.
revision_notes: Sources fetched and confirmed: the Civil Status Act establishes the civil registration and NIN framework, compulsory since 1995 per the 2022 budget address; the Data Protection Act 2023 provides a comprehensive legal framework for digital identity data. A further search confirmed via the official 2023 budget address and Biometric Update coverage that the SeyID electronic ID platform became operational at the end of October/1 November 2022 as a key component of the government's Digital Economy Agenda. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed, no change.
revised_comments: Seychelles' digital identity is underpinned by formal legislation. The Civil Status Act governs civil registration and the National Identity Number, compulsory since 1995, while the Data Protection Act 2023 provides a comprehensive legal framework for the processing of digital identity data, including biometric information collected under the SeyID platform, which became operational at the end of October 2022 as a key component of the government's Digital Economy Agenda.

Definition: Whether the Ministry of Finance has oversight of the financing and development of the digital ID system
Comments: The Ministry of Finance plays a partial oversight role. The 2022 budget speech by Finance Minister Naadir Hassan explicitly referred to the SeyID system as 'key to the Digital Economy Agenda', allocated R145.1 million in 2023 for ICT projects, and announced priorities for SeyID platform integration. The World Bank Digital Government report recommended giving DICT 'a Ministry of Finance backed power to veto spending on technology projects' — suggesting this power was not yet fully formalised. Finance oversees budgetary allocations but full formal oversight mechanism is not confirmed.
revision_notes: Sources fetched and confirmed, including a full read of the 2022/2023 budget address (the originally cited nation.sc URL contains a typo in its slug, 'minister-for-ownership' instead of 'minister-for-finance', but the article ID resolves correctly to the intended budget speech). The address confirms the electronic ID system became operational in October 2022 as the key element of the Digital Economy Agenda, with R145.1 million allocated over the medium term for ICT/digital projects, and a further search found that the Minister for Finance chairs the Digital Economy Steering Committee overseeing SeyID and related digital projects. The World Bank's 'Digital Government in Seychelles' report recommends, rather than confirms as existing, giving DICT a Ministry-of-Finance-backed veto power over technology spending, indicating budgetary but not full formal oversight. Score of 2 (Partial oversight) confirmed, no change.
revised_comments: The Ministry of Finance, National Planning and Trade exercises partial oversight of Seychelles' digital ID financing and development. The Minister chairs the government's Digital Economy Steering Committee, under which the SeyID platform operates, and the Ministry allocates budget for ICT and digital-economy projects, including R145.1 million over the medium term for digital economy infrastructure. A World Bank review has recommended granting the Ministry formal veto power over technology spending across departments, indicating that comprehensive, formalised financial oversight of the ID system is not yet fully in place.

Definition: Whether the system collects biometric data and which modalities are collected (fingerprints, facial image, iris scans)
Comments: Seychelles collects both facial and fingerprint biometrics. The biometric passport introduced in November 2022 includes an electronic chip with facial recognition and fingerprint data. The SeyID eKYC process uses facial video selfie for verification. The National Population Database contains biographic and photographic data. Biometric passports are produced by IN Groupe with full biometric collection at enrollment stations.
revision_notes: Sources fetched and confirmed: the biometric e-passport, launched November 2022 and produced by IN Groupe, embeds an electronic chip containing facial image and fingerprint data; the SeyID eKYC process separately captures a facial video selfie for identity verification. Score of 3 (Facial/Iris) confirmed, no change.
revised_comments: Seychelles collects both facial and fingerprint biometric data. The biometric e-passport, introduced in November 2022 and produced by IN Groupe, embeds an electronic chip containing the holder's facial image and fingerprints. Separately, the SeyID digital identity platform's eKYC process captures a live facial video selfie for identity verification.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for SIM card activation and mobile service registration
Comments: SIM card registration requiring national ID is mandatory in Seychelles. A December 2020 Seychelles Nation article describes stricter SIM registration regulations: carriers must verify and record customer personally identifiable information prior to SIM activation; unregistered SIMs were deactivated by January 2021. PikaSim (2026) confirms 'Seychelles requires national ID or passport registration for SIM cards. Carriers must maintain customer identification records under telecommunications regulations.' National ID or passport is the required document.
revision_notes: Sources fetched and confirmed: Seychelles Nation (16 December 2020) reports that mandatory registration and verification of personally identifiable information became a precondition of SIM activation, with unregistered SIMs subject to deactivation from 27 January 2021; PikaSim (2026), a commercial eSIM reseller, corroborates that national ID or passport registration remains mandatory for SIM cards under current telecommunications regulations. The 2020 government-sourced article is treated as the primary authority; PikaSim is a lower-authority commercial source used only as corroboration of continuity. Score of 3 (Mandatory) confirmed, no change.
revised_comments: SIM card registration in Seychelles is mandatory and requires presentation of a national ID card or passport. Regulations introduced in December 2020 require telecommunications operators to verify and record customers' identification information before activating a SIM, with unregistered accounts subject to deactivation; this requirement remains in force.
